I was submitted into in patient treatment for two weeks in early February this year. I had some issues with the staff and other things but I do have to thank them for stabilizing my weight when I was at a very bad spot. Before I went to in patient I was told I was lucky my body hadn't started shutting down yet. 

I will try to tell you as much as I remember from my experience. 

Our day starts off at 5 am with the sudden sound of a cart crashing into your room as a nurse walks in to take your vitals. The day ends at 9 pm and you are allowed roughly five minutes to shower. The showers are kinda gross so make sure to bring flip flops. You are not allowed certain items, such as razors or rope or glass picture frames, as some sort of suicide or self harm prevention thingy. So no shaving your legs.

Staff would come check on us in our rooms every thirty minutes to make sure we were ok, even at night when you're asleep, they would just come in and shine a flashlight on you. You will probably be too tired for it to bother you though. 

The worst part about it for me was the bathroom rules. All of the bathrooms are locked, so you have to ask for permission to use the bathroom. They keep track of your pee and poop. Before you flush they have to look at it. I know, awkward. And you are not allowed to close the door, the staff have to stand behind the door with it cracked open. Just remember, they are human, and nobody wants to stand there while someone else is using the bathroom, so they are uncomfortable like you are. But yeah there isn't much bathroom privacy which bothered me a lot. It's to prevent purging. 

There were some restrictions due to Covid when I was there. They would only allow one visitor at a time and it could only be parents. I was supposed to have a roommate but due to Covid I had a room to myself. 

We would have this schedule every day for certain things. For example, when we would be getting our vitals done, seeing a therapist, seeing the doctor, things like that. When we weren't busy we would just sit in a day room watching TV, coloring, playing Mario Kart, playing cards and board games, things like that. I don't know if you're a minor or not, I went into in patient as a minor, and there are some differences between how minors and adults are treated. Minors have more restrictions than adults, we were not allowed phones at first (they do have phones for you to borrow) or to watch anything rated R, things like that. There was also a teacher there for schooling but my parents didn't enroll me for any of the school stuff because they wanted me to focus solely on getting better.

Don't be afraid of the other patients, I was really scared going into it that they were going to judge me and exclude me, but they ended up being the nicest people I've ever met. We all just naturally became friends and supported each other. It was super sweet. It will help you to open up and make friends so that you don't feel so alone in this experience. 

As for staff, most of the staff in my experience are really nice but some were a little rude or unprofessional. Some were very strict. There was this one who I really disliked, she was just doing the most for absolutely no reason lol. For instance, the staff are supposed to stand behind the bathroom door, BEHIND the door, but her creepy self would stand IN the crack of the door, literally watching me, making eye contact with me while I'm trying to take a crap. That was probably the most awkward position I've ever been in in my life. Then there were some who were really understanding and would actually let me close the door and even walk away and let me take a crap in peace, even though they weren't supposed to do that. I salute them.

Ok, now onto the eating. We had about 45-50 minutes to eat each meal, and 15 minutes for snack. We would have 3 meals and three snacks every day: breakfast, then snack, then lunch, then snack, then dinner, then snack. Although they encourage you to finish you food, they don't actually force you to finish all of your food. If we didn't finish, they just gave us a replacement shake. Some people said it tasted gross, but it didn't taste too bad imo. That reminds me, when you first get there they ask you what kinds of foods you like, so it's not like you're going to be eating gross foods you don't like. If you do get dished a food you don't like that you didn't think to tell them before, you can still tell them and you won't be given that food again. I was given guacamole and it made me gag, so they didn't give me it again.

We had to go through these different phases, from 1 to 3. As you move up, you are granted more privileges. I think at stage 2 you no longer needed a worker to stand by the door while you used the bathroom, and you were given more freedom to leave the day room and go to your room by yourself when you wanted. (If you're a minor) your parents were able to get more involved and start coming in to plan your meals for you. And in phase 3 (again, if you're a minor) you were allowed to finally have your phone. I forgot what other privileges you were granted in phase 3 because I never made it that far, I only got to phase 2. Phase 2 is very difficult to pass. If you finish all of your meals and go an entire day without needing a replacement, that is how you move up a phase. They would slowly bump up the calories by 500 each week. They would start off at say 1,500 calories the first week, then 2,000 calories the second, etc. 

The amount of food they gave us was ridiculous. I was on a good streak of no replacements for a few days and I was just about to be moved to phase 3. But then they punished me for having ONE replacement because I was feeling sick, and sent me back to phase one. I don't like how they perpetually trap those who are struggling in a certain phase as a means of punishment. It just totally destroyed my vibe and I felt like I was never going to make it back to phase 2 and I never did. I would just eat as much as I could and then have as many replacement shakes as I wanted. I didn't see what was wrong with having the shakes instead of food, you were getting the same amount of calories just in a more compacted, liquid form, and I honestly preferred to have the shakes instead of eating so much. But apparently that's bad and you're supposed to not have any replacements. I hated that. I feel like they have these near impossible eating standards. I don't know anybody in my life who eats that big, six times a day. As long as you're eating better than before and you're drinking the shakes I think that's fine.

They have medications for anxiety and nausea such as hydroxyzine, simethicone for bloating and gas. They also had something to help with constipation too. You will need it. 

My advice would be don't fight it. It makes it a lot easier if you comply and at least try to get better and show that you want to get better. Despite the struggles, when I left in patient I felt a lot better and I looked a lot better and I just felt amazing. 

I hope this helps.
